issues.item: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising Others' is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile and the trauma type. The other items center on childhood physical abuse, mistrust, touch-sensitivity, fragmented memory, guilt, and self-damage; obsessive worry about harm befalling loved ones points to a different threat theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' suggests a home-intrusion/security threat theme. In this profile, threat is otherwise expressed as interpersonal danger cues (unexpected touch, ominous silence) linked to caregiver abuse. Without matching appraisals or memory content about break-ins or external intruders, this item is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Leo was fifty-five, a fashion designer who had built a career on precision and control, but the foundation beneath him had always been fractured. When he was a boy, his father's discipline had been a fist, a belt, a cold silence that could turn into a storm without warning. The worst night, when he was nine, had started over a half-finished homework assignment. His father had grabbed him by the collar, slammed him against the wall, and kept hitting until Leo stopped crying. He remembered the drywall cracking behind his head, the smell of his father's whiskey breath, and the strange, hollow feeling afterward-like watching a movie of someone else's life. Even now, he could not tell the story in a straight line. Pieces were missing, and when he tried to recall it, he sometimes felt nothing at all, as if it had happened to a stranger. But other times, the guilt would surge up, a sickening wave: he should have done the homework earlier, should have been better, should have made his father proud.

That guilt had become a habit. He dwelled on what he had done wrong, replaying the night in his head, searching for the moment he could have avoided it. But he also dwelled on what his father had done, spinning the same angry loop: the injustice, the cruelty, the way his father had never apologized. This rumination was not a choice anymore; it was a groove in his mind. He had come to believe that the abuse had permanently damaged him, that he had changed for the worse, and that people could not be trusted. These beliefs felt like facts. Because he was broken, he told himself, he deserved to be alone. Because people were untrustworthy, he kept them at arm's length. His divorce had only confirmed this. His ex-wife had said he was cold, unreachable-and she was right. He was certain that his reactions since the abuse meant he was going crazy, and that thought only drove him deeper into the same mental ruts.

The rumination fed on itself, but it also fed the threat he felt everywhere. At his studio, a long table of silk and sketches, he worked with assistants who moved quietly. An unusual silence would make his stomach tighten, a signal that something dangerous was about to happen. He felt on guard even inside his own home, a loft he had designed to feel open and safe, but it never did. When someone touched him unexpectedly-a hand on his shoulder, a brush in a crowd-he would flinch, his heart hammering before his mind could catch up. These moments of alarm would yank him back to the memory of his father's hands, and the memory would confirm that he was right to be afraid, that the world was still dangerous. The threat and the memory circled each other, each one making the other more vivid, more real.

He had developed small strategies to manage the nightmares. He avoided certain times of day-late afternoons, when the light slanted like it had on that night-and he kept a strict routine before bed to steer his mind away from the dreams. But these strategies only reinforced his sense that he was fragile, that he had to be careful, that he was permanently damaged. The rumination, the avoidance, the hypervigilance-they all told the same story: he was not okay, and he never would be.

For years, he had managed. He designed collections, attended fittings, smiled at clients. But last month, at a fabric show, a buyer had tapped his elbow from behind. Leo had spun around, his fist half-clenched, his face white. The buyer had stepped back, embarrassed. Leo had laughed it off, but afterward he could not stop replaying the moment, could not stop feeling the guilt and the anger and the fear. That night, he dreamed of his father's hands again. The next morning, he called a therapist. He was not sure what he was hoping for-maybe just to stop feeling like he was falling apart. But what frightened him most was the possibility that nothing could change, that the damage was permanent, and that he would spend the rest of his life jumping at shadows in his own home.
